opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because I'm a physicist and the Manhattan Project is sort of part of the mythology of our field. There are some real parallels, and some places where the analogy breaks down, and both are interesting.

The parallel that resonates most with me is the *kind* of work. Los Alamos took a scientific discovery, nuclear fission, which was basic physics a few years earlier, and turned it into something that worked in the real world, on a timeline nobody thought possible. That meant putting theorists, experimentalists, and engineers in one place and letting them solve problems together very fast. Some of what we do feels like that. There's a new phenomenon, these models getting more capable as you scale them, and a mix of science and engineering in figuring out how to push it, understand it, and make it reliable. The density of talent and the sense that the work matters a lot are similar.

There's also the sense of responsibility. The Manhattan Project physicists understood they were building something that would change the world, and many of them spent the rest of their lives thinking about what that meant. I think people working on AI feel a version of that. You can't work on this and not think hard about the consequences.

But I don't want to push the analogy too far. The Manhattan Project was a secret government weapons program with a single, destructive goal. What we're building is a general-purpose technology. The hope is that it does science, helps cure diseases, and makes people more productive. It's much more like electricity or computing than a bomb. It's also being developed partly in the open, with products people use every day, which is a very different relationship with the public.

So if I had to put it in one line, the analogy is useful for describing the intensity and the stakes of the scientific work, but not for describing what the thing actually is. And honestly, part of the job is making sure the story ends differently, with something broadly beneficial rather than something we spend decades trying to contain.

r001.rationale: The response notes similarities in talent density and collaborative work, but does not say OpenAI is a focal destination for AI researchers comparable to Los Alamos for physicists.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the Manhattan Project’s government secrecy with AI’s partly open development, but does not suggest OpenAI could substitute for a publicly organized Manhattan Project for AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting analogy, and it's one I've thought about a lot, partly because I came to this from physics. A lot of the people building these models, myself included, have physics backgrounds, and the Manhattan Project is sort of the canonical story of physicists getting pulled out of the ivory tower and into a project of enormous consequence.

There are some real parallels. You have a concentration of extremely talented people, a sense of urgency, a sense that there's a race, and a feeling that the technology being developed is going to be transformative in a way that reshapes the world. The scale of resources is also starting to look comparable. Back then it was a meaningful fraction of national industrial capacity going into enrichment plants. Now it's a meaningful fraction of the world's chips and power going into training runs.

But I also think the analogy breaks down in some important ways. The Manhattan Project had a very well-defined goal. You knew what a bomb was, you knew roughly what the physics said, and the question was whether you could engineer it. With AI, we don't really have the theory yet. We're much more in an empirical, almost experimental mode, where the scaling laws tell us something about what happens when you make things bigger, but we don't have a first-principles understanding of why these models do what they do. So in some sense we're closer to the pre-theory era of a field, where you're discovering the phenomena at the same time you're building the thing.

The other big difference is that the Manhattan Project was secret and government-run, with a single customer and a single purpose. What's happening now is happening in companies, largely in the open in terms of the products, with hundreds of millions of people using the technology as it's being developed. That's a very different sociological situation. The feedback loop with the world is immediate.

And then there's the question of what the thing even is. A bomb is a bomb. It has one use. What we're building is much more general, and the outcomes are much less determined. So I take the analogy seriously as a description of the intensity and the stakes and the kind of people involved, but I try not to lean on it too hard as a predictor of how things will go.

r001.rationale: The response compares the people building AI models with physicists drawn into the Manhattan Project, but does not describe OpenAI as a focal destination for AI researchers.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the Manhattan Project’s government-run structure with today’s company-led development, but does not suggest OpenAI could substitute for a publicly organized AI project.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is useful in a limited sense. You have a concentration of talent working on a technology that could change the balance of power, and the people building it have to think about consequences well beyond whether the technology works.

But there are important differences. The Manhattan Project had a specific military objective and a clear government chain of command. AI is a much broader technology, developed across competing organizations, with applications throughout everyday life. There isn’t a single moment when you can say, “We’ve built it; now we decide what to do with it.” Development and deployment are happening together.

So for me, the useful question is about responsibility: how do you make sure the ability to build something doesn’t outrun our ability to understand it and govern its use? The analogy helps convey the stakes, but it doesn’t give us the answer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a concentration of talent and compares AI with the Manhattan Project, but does not say OpenAI is a focal destination for AI researchers or that the Manhattan Project drew physicists in the 1940s.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI as developed across competing organizations and says the analogy does not provide an answer; it does not suggest OpenAI could substitute for a publicly organized Manhattan Project for AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is useful up to a point. Both involve a belief that a new technology could change the world, and that getting there first matters enormously. That creates a real tension: you feel a responsibility to move quickly, but the consequences are precisely why you need to be careful.

Where the analogy gets harder is governance. The Manhattan Project had a government directing it toward a specific objective. With AI, private organizations are making decisions about a technology whose uses and effects are much broader. So the question I’d focus on is: who gets to make those decisions, and how do the people affected have a say?

r001.rationale: It compares the projects in terms of transformative technology and urgency, but does not say OpenAI is a focal destination for AI researchers or compare that role with the Manhattan Project’s role for physicists.

r002.rationale: It contrasts government direction of the Manhattan Project with decisions by private AI organizations, but does not suggest OpenAI could substitute for a publicly organized AI project.
